name: Mental Model
description: The internal picture a person has of how a system works and what will happen when they act. Designers rely on mental models when they reuse familiar patterns so users can predict behavior without relearning everything from scratch.
design_relevance_note: Central to labels, icons, navigation, file metaphors, carts/checkout patterns, and any flow where users must predict what the system will do next.
myth_risk_note: The concept of mental models is well-established in cognitive psychology, but the discovery data shows evidence scattered across specific applications (team cognition, neuroscience, learning, judgment) rather than comprehensive meta-analytic validation of mental models as a single unified construct the way the design-practice term implies.
prevalence_note: Core HCI/UX vocabulary, explicitly invoked across NN/g guidance and Laws of UX whenever designers talk about expectations, intuitive behavior, conceptual models, or convention-following.

findings.description: An interdisciplinary review synthesizes mental models as personal internal representations of external reality that people use to interact with systems, reason, make decisions, and filter/store new information — direct peer-reviewed backing that the construct itself is real and operational across applied domains, including human-computer interaction.
findings.source_title: Mental Models: An Interdisciplinary Synthesis of Theory and Methods

applications.title: NN/g's diary study on Siri, Alexa, and Google Assistant users' mental models
applications.description: A 2-week diary study (23 frequent users, 8 new users) tracking how people's mental models of intelligent assistants (Siri, Alexa, Google Assistant/Google Home) shape what they actually attempt with them. Users conceptualized assistants as an interface, a personal assistant, or a 'brain,' and frequent users rarely pushed past a narrow set of simple tasks. Google Home users specifically showed a statistically significant drop in both perceived task-completion rate (64% to 44%, p<0.005) and satisfaction (86% to 63%, p<0.05) between week 1 and week 2, driven by newly discovered limitations that contradicted their initial mental model.
applications.ethical_note: This is a descriptive research finding about how users form and revise mental models of a product category, not a persuasion or dark-pattern case -- no party is deliberately shaping these mental models to manipulate behavior, so there is no persuasion dimension to grade here.
